message.content:
**Answer**

The last common ancestor of a lion (*Panthera leo*) and a zebra (*Equus quagga*) was a small, insectivorous mammal that lived roughly 70–80 million years ago during the late Paleocene–early Eocene. This ancestor belonged to the clade **Laurasiatheria**, the group that gave rise to all of the placental mammals that live on the northern continents today (Carnivora, Perissodactyla, Artiodactyla, Chiroptera, Cetartiodactyla, etc.). In other words, the lion and zebra share a common ancestor that is a member of the Laurasiatherian lineage, which existed long before the split between the Felidae (cats) and Equidae (horses, zebras, donkeys).

Their last common ancestor would be a common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla? Actually lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in order Perissodactyla. The last common ancestor of all mammals? But maybe they want the most recent common ancestor of the two species. That would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae. That would be a common ancestor of the clade that includes both Felidae and Equidae. That clade is the clade that includes all placental mammals? Actually Felidae and Equidae diverged early in the evolution of placental mammals. The last common ancestor of Felidae and Equidae would be a member of the clade that includes the superorders Laurasiatheria? Wait, Felidae is part of the superorder Laurasiatheria, within the clade of carnivores. Equidae is also part of Laurasiatheria, within Perissodactyla. So the last common ancestor of Felidae and Equidae would be a member of Laurasiatheria, perhaps a member of the clade that includes the ancestors of all Laurasiatherian mammals. That would be a mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is older (~100-120 million years). But the last common ancestor of Felidae and Equidae is likely a member of the clade that gave rise to the Laurasiatheria, which includes orders like Carnivora, Perissodactyla, Artiodactyla, Chiroptera, Cetartiodactyla, etc. So the answer: The last common ancestor of lion and zebra was a mammal that lived about 70-80 million years ago, belonging to the Laurasiatheria clade. It might have been a small, insectivorous mammal. But we can say: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras is a member of the Laurasiatheria clade, which existed around 70-80 million years ago. Alternatively, we could mention the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is a member of the clade that includes the ancestors of all placental mammals. But the question likely expects: The common ancestor of lion and zebra is the common ancestor of all mammals, or the last common ancestor of the two species is a mammal that lived in the Paleocene/Eocene. But the question might be answered simply: The common ancestor of lion and zebra is a mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago, belonging to the Laurasiatheria clade. Or we can say: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras is a member of the clade that gave rise to the Laurasiatheria, which includes the ancestors of all placental mammals. But we can also mention that the last common ancestor of the two species is a member of the clade that includes the ancestors of all placental mammals, but more specifically, the last common ancestor of the two families is a member of the Laurasiatheria clade.
